If you ever want to get formal with Claude.
Claude Code is good at individual tasks. But once you start doing serious work, sessions that involve complex workflows, iterative planning, real artefacts, the same friction points keep appearing.

Workflows produce things: plans, drafts, designs, structured outputs. Reviewing them inline in a running conversation is awkward. You scroll, copy-paste, lose your place, then have to re-inject your decisions back into the session. There's no natural pause point.

You've built workflows that work. But remembering the exact invocation, the right command, the right context, the right flags, is its own cognitive tax every time. You spend energy on the meta-work of starting work.

Some tasks are sequential. Many aren't. But the default mode in a Claude Code session is linear. Planning what can run concurrently and what has to wait, then executing that plan without losing track, is harder than it should be.
Debussy is a meta-plugin: a plugin about using the plugin ecosystem better. It doesn't replace anything. It adds a thin layer of structure on top of whatever you're already doing with Claude Code.
The name is a small joke. Claude Debussy, the composer, was known for structure beneath apparent improvisation. That felt right.
Three things, in order of how often the friction appears:
An artefact review interface. A proper UI to review what a workflow just produced. Accept, reject, annotate, then feed the decisions back into the session.
A workflow launcher. A menu of the workflows you actually use, so launching one is a single action instead of a recall exercise.
A parallel planner. A structured way to plan a session before running it, what runs in sequence, what can be dispatched concurrently, and track execution as it happens.
